frame.claim: A coordinate frame is a measuring rig: an origin point plus a set of mutually perpendicular unit direction vectors (axes). It is not a plane — a point in space exists regardless of any frame, and only gets numbers once you measure it against some frame.
frame.probe: A friend who has never met coordinate systems says 'a frame is like a plane.' Explain what a frame really is: name its two ingredients, correct the plane misunderstanding, and say whether a physical point can have coordinates without any frame at all.
rubric: names both ingredients: an origin (reference point) and a set of mutually perpendicular unit direction vectors (axes)
corrects the 'plane' idea — a frame is a measuring rig, not a surface
states coordinates exist only relative to some frame, while the point itself is frame-independent

viz.hint: Static canvas: a point in empty space; fade in a labeled origin + two axis arrows and watch numbers appear only when the frame does.

point-in-frame.claim: A point's coordinates in a frame are the signed distances you travel along that frame's axes from its origin to reach the point — so the same physical point has different numbers in different frames.
point-in-frame.probe: You've drawn two frames on graph paper: Frame A with its origin at the page corner, axes pointing right and up; Frame B with its origin 2 squares right of A's origin, axes pointing the same directions. A dot sits 3 squares right and 4 squares up from A's origin. What are the dot's coordinates in A, and in B? Then explain in one sentence what a coordinate pair is measuring.
rubric: A-coordinates: (3, 4)
B-coordinates: (1, 4) — origin offset subtracted
explains coordinates as signed distances walked along the frame's axes from its origin

viz.hint: Canvas with two labeled frames and a draggable dot; live readout in both frames — drag the dot (or the B frame) and watch only the numbers move, never the point.

world-frame.claim: The world frame is the one fixed frame you declare by choice (conventionally at the robot base, x right, y up) and never move; every other frame's position and orientation are ultimately described relative to it.
world-frame.probe: An arm's base sits at the corner of your workbench and you are told to 'use the world frame'. What do you physically choose and place? Why is it acceptable that this choice is arbitrary? And what would be wrong with using the moving shoulder joint itself as the world frame?
rubric: chooses an origin (bench corner or base) and fixed axis directions (e.g., x right, y up)
states the choice is arbitrary but once made it must not move — everything else is measured against it
explains the moving-frame failure: a world frame that rides the shoulder would give the arm changing coordinates even when nothing physical moves

viz.hint: Static scene: bench, arm base at origin, world axes drawn and labeled; caption asks 'what breaks if this frame moves?'

link-frame.claim: A link frame is a frame bolted to a moving link: it rotates with the link, so points rigidly attached to the link keep constant coordinates in the link's own frame while their world coordinates change as joints move.
link-frame.probe: A sensor is welded to the end of a link at coordinates (0.30, 0.00) in the frame painted on that link. The joint at the link's base then rotates 45°. What happens to the sensor's coordinates in the link's own frame, and what happens to its coordinates in the world frame? Explain why the two answers differ.
rubric: link-frame coordinates stay (0.30, 0.00) — unchanged
world coordinates change when the joint rotates
explains why: the link frame is rigidly attached to the link, so anything welded to the link is stationary in it, while the world frame is not

viz.hint: 2-link arm with joint sliders and a coordinate table: elbow and tip in world vs each link frame — the local columns freeze while the world numbers spin.

contrast.deep_feature: whether the frame a point is described in is rigidly attached to the moving body that holds the point
cases: Elbow position written in the world frame; the shoulder motor then turns 30°.
Elbow position written in the frame painted on link 1 (x-axis along the upper arm); the shoulder motor then turns 30°.
Pen-tip position written in the frame painted on link 2 (x-axis along the forearm); the elbow motor then turns 45°.
Pen-tip position written in the world frame; the elbow motor then turns 45°.
contrast.invite: For each of the four cases, decide: does the written coordinate pair change or stay the same when the motor turns? Then state one rule that predicts all four answers.

transform-frame.claim: To express a point known in frame B in frame A: first rotate the B-coordinates by the angle between the frames, then add the position of B's origin measured in A (p_A = R(θ)·p_B + t).
transform-frame.probe: Frame B is rotated 30° counterclockwise from Frame A, and B's origin sits at (0.20, 0.10) in A. A point P has coordinates (0.40, 0.00) in B. Write the transform equation first, then compute P's coordinates in Frame A, showing your work.
rubric: setup: writes p_A = R(θ)·p_B + t — rotation applied first, translation second
rotation step: (0.40, 0.00) rotated by 30° gives (0.346, 0.200)
translation step: adds B's origin (0.20, 0.10)
final answer ≈ (0.546, 0.300)

viz.hint: Step-through animation of a point crossing frames: spin B's coordinate axes first, then slide by B's origin — the two motions must never merge into one.

practice.problem_frame: Given two frames with a known relative rotation and translation, convert a point's coordinates from one frame to the other.
practice.discriminates_from: Adding the translation before the rotation, or rotating by the wrong direction of angle.
practice.verify: Convert the point back the other way (rotate by −θ, subtract t) and confirm you return to the original coordinates.
error_bank: applying rotation and translation in the wrong order
sign error on the rotation angle between frames

fk-chain.claim: Forward kinematics chains frames: express the elbow in the world frame, then take the tip's offset in link 2's frame and rotate it by the accumulated angle θ1+θ2: tip_world = R(θ1)·(L1, 0) + R(θ1+θ2)·(L2, 0).
fk-chain.probe: A planar 2-link arm: L1 = 0.4 m, L2 = 0.3 m, shoulder angle θ1 = 30° measured from the world x-axis, elbow angle θ2 = 45° measured from the direction of link 1. Draw the frame diagram and compute the tip's world coordinates, showing every step, then sanity-check the answer (signs, tip farther from base than elbow?).
rubric: diagram: world frame at the base; link frames drawn on both links, link 2's frame oriented at θ1 + θ2 = 75° from the world x-axis
chaining step: elbow in world = R(30°)·(0.4, 0) = (0.346, 0.200)
tip offset uses the total angle θ1 + θ2 = 75°, not θ2 alone: adds (0.3·cos75°, 0.3·sin75°) = (0.078, 0.290)
final tip ≈ (0.424, 0.490), sanity-checked (both positive, tip farther from base than elbow)

viz.hint: Arm with θ1 and θ2 sliders, ghost elbow marker, and a highlighted 'θ1+θ2' arc at the hand — the forearm's world orientation is the accumulated angle.

practice.problem_frame: Given a planar 2-link arm's lengths and joint angles, compute the tip's world coordinates via chained frame transforms.
practice.discriminates_from: Using θ2 alone for the forearm's world orientation instead of θ1+θ2.
practice.verify: Check the tip position against a sketch: tip must lie on the correct side of the elbow and beyond it along the forearm direction.
error_bank: elbow step missed — going straight to the tip from the base
forearm rotated by θ2 instead of θ1+θ2
length units mixed or angles in degrees in a radian formula

motion-ik.claim: IK finds joint angles for a desired tip pose, and a 2-DOF planar arm has two solutions — elbow-up and elbow-down. The Jacobian loses rank at singularities (arm straight out: the elbow can't help). Plan in task space, control in joint space; min-jerk trajectories avoid infinite jerk at start/stop.
motion-ik.probe: Arm with L1 = L2 = 0.4 m, tip at (0.6, 0.3). Sketch the two IK solutions. Why is the arm at full extension singular? Where do you plan the path versus where do you control it, and why the split? Why does a min-jerk profile beat a trapezoid for first motion?
rubric: two solutions drawn (elbow-up / elbow-down), roughly mirrored about the base-to-target axis
singularity at full extension: Jacobian rank drops — no elbow authority along that direction
task-space planning → joint-space control split
min-jerk: bounded jerk at trajectory start/stop (ideal trapezoid commands unbounded jerk spikes)

pendulum-dynamics.claim: Dynamics is the free-body law with motion: ΣF = ma, Στ = Iα. Simulation is a model with assumptions — friction, inertias, delays — and sim-vs-reality gaps are a fingerprint of what the model forgot. Build the sim first, then reconcile: identical inputs, compare outputs, find the unmodeled term.
pendulum-dynamics.probe: Your sim says a pendulum reaches 60° in 1.2 s; the real one takes 1.5 s. List three candidate unmodeled effects in order of likelihood and the measurement that would confirm each — and state the testing discipline that governs how you run each check.
rubric: friction/damping in the joint (measure: coast-down or step response decay)
inertia of rotor/drivetrain not in the model (measure: known added mass)
sensor or command latency (measure: step-response delay)
method: change one thing, compare to sim each time

pendulum-cart.claim: The inverted pendulum is the canonical unstable plant: any perturbation grows unless the controller acts faster than the instability's timescale. Linearize about the upright, build the state-space model, and LQR picks the gains — the cart fights gravity through the pole. It is Phase 2's proof that model → simulate → LQR → hardware works end to end.
pendulum-cart.probe: Why is the upright position unstable in the first place? What must the controller do faster than? Name the LQR state vector and why the pole's angular rate matters.
rubric: instability: gravity torque grows the displacement; no natural restoring force
controller must act faster than the instability timescale
state vector: x, v, θ, θ̇ — the rate terms make the controller anticipate
LQR weights trade pole-angle effort against cart travel

bond-graph.claim: Bond graphs are a cross-domain energy language: every physical system is effort × flow = power — voltage × current, force × velocity, torque × angular velocity. Elements: sources (effort or flow), storage (C: spring/capacitor, I: mass/inductor), dissipation (R), and transducers — a motor is a gyrator coupling electrical effort to mechanical flow, and energy conservation gives Kt = Ke.
bond-graph.probe: Model a motor driving a load as a bond graph: name the effort and flow on the electrical side and the mechanical side, the two energy-storage elements, and the transducer. Where does the equality Kt = Ke come from?
rubric: electrical: effort = voltage, flow = current; mechanical: effort = torque, flow = angular velocity
storage: inductor/capacitor on the electrical side, inertia/spring on the mechanical side
motor as gyrator coupling the two domains
Kt = Ke from power/energy conservation in the transducer

viz.hint: A motor-load bond graph you can drag elements onto; each bond shows effort × flow with live power numbers, and the gyrator flips effort/flow roles.

bond-graph.transfer_probe: A bicycle turns leg effort into motion: pedals and chain transmit power, the hill stores and returns energy, brakes dissipate it. Name the effort and flow on the leg side and the wheel side, the storage and dissipation elements, and the transducer — where is the Kt = Ke analogue?

impedance-haptic.claim: Impedance control makes a joint feel like a spring-damper written in software: τ = Kp(θd − θ) + Kd(ωd − ω). The haptic knob's 'feel' is virtual dynamics — stiffer spring = more torque per position error, damping = resistance to motion. The device can only present impedance within its physical capability: torque limits and bandwidth bound the feel you can fake.
impedance-haptic.probe: A knob should feel like a 1 N·m/rad spring. Write the control law, say which term makes it feel springy and which makes it feel smooth, give the physical limit that would make the feel 'fake' — and what happens to the feel if the position sensor dies?
rubric: τ = Kp(θd − θ) + Kd(ωd − ω) with stiffness Kp
Kp = spring feel, Kd = damping feel
torque/bandwidth limits: beyond available torque or update rate, the feel breaks
no sensor, no feel — feedback is the illusion

harness-workcell.claim: A harness is a system you can debug: every wire labeled, strain relief at every connector, twisted pairs for signal, and a return path that never loops through the frame. EMI is fought at the cable — shield and drain — not in software. The workcell convention: bundle by function, color-code by voltage, and the harness drawing is a deliverable, not a doodle.
harness-workcell.probe: Your arm's encoder is glitchy only when the motor is commanded. Give the three cable-level causes in order and the fix for each. What does 'return path' mean and why does the frame count as a bad one? What drawing deliverables prove the harness is right?
rubric: inductive coupling from motor leads — separate/route motor away from signal
ground loop through the frame — use dedicated return, not structure
missing shield/twisted pair with proper drain termination
harness drawing + labels as deliverables

gripper-toolchanger.claim: A tool changer is a mechanical + electrical contract: pogo pins mate power and signal at a defined stroke; kinematic alignment (cones/V-grooves) gives repeatability without precision machining; and the change sequence is a state machine — release → move → dock → confirm. Interfaces are contracts: define the port and payload before building either side.
gripper-toolchanger.probe: Why pogo pins and not a connector? Why kinematic (cone/V-groove) alignment instead of tight tolerances? Write the tool-change state sequence and the confirm step that makes it safe. When in the program must the interface contract be frozen?
rubric: pogo pins: spring-loaded, tolerant of misalignment, defined wipe/stroke
kinematic coupling: repeatability from geometry, not machining precision
state sequence: release → move → dock → confirm (electrical check)
interface contract defined before either side is built

motion-ik-singularity.claim: At full extension the 2-link arm's Jacobian loses rank, so the elbow joint contributes nothing along the arm's axis and one direction of tip-motion authority is lost.
motion-ik-singularity.probe: A planar 2-link arm is stretched straight out (elbow fully extended, θ2 = 0) and you command a small tip motion straight outward along the arm's axis. What happens to the tip, which joint can and cannot contribute to that motion, and what does this say about the Jacobian's columns and rank at this pose?
rubric: states the outward motion along the arm axis is instantaneously impossible: small joint changes move the tip sideways only
identifies the elbow as contributing nothing along the arm axis at full extension
frames it as Jacobian rank loss: the columns align and become dependent, so rank drops from 2 to 1
motion-ik-singularity.transfer_probe: A two-hinge folding solar wing sits unfolded perfectly flat when ground control asks its outer edge to nudge 2 cm farther straight outward along the wing's own plane. Which hinge motor can contribute to that motion, what happens to the edge instead, and what is the flat-wing analogue of Jacobian rank loss?

motion-ik-solutions.claim: For a reachable interior target of a 2-link planar arm, inverse kinematics has two solutions, elbow-up and elbow-down, mirrored about the line from base to target.
motion-ik-solutions.probe: A planar 2-link arm has L1 = L2 = 0.4 m and must place its tip at (0.6, 0.3) in the world frame. Sketch the two different arm postures that reach it. For each posture, say roughly where the elbow is, how the two elbow positions relate to each other geometrically, and what computation with the joint angles (or elbow position) would confirm the tip really lands on (0.6, 0.3).
rubric: gives two distinct postures with the elbows on opposite sides of the base-to-target line, each about 0.4 m from the base and about 0.4 m from the target
states the geometric relation: the two elbow positions are mirror images across the line from the base to the target
names the verifying computation and its result: forward kinematics of each solution's angles (or the segment-length checks) reproduces the tip at approximately (0.6, 0.3)
motion-ik-solutions.transfer_probe: A two-segment desk lamp (two 15-cm arms) must hold its bulb over one ink dot on a notebook. Name the two postures the lamp can take, how the two elbow positions mirror each other, and the measurement that would confirm both really place the bulb over the dot.

motion-ik-taskspace.claim: Straight-line tip motion is specified in task space but executed by joint-space servos fed through IK along the path, and smooth rest-to-rest moves use a min-jerk profile with finitely ramping acceleration rather than the ideal trapezoid's stepwise acceleration switches, which in the ideal model demand unbounded jerk spikes.
motion-ik-taskspace.probe: You want a two-joint arm's tip to draw a straight 20-cm line on a table. The line is trivial to write as x-y waypoints, but each motor only reports its own shaft angle. Where do you specify the waypoints, where do the motor commands get computed and closed, and why can't you do the whole job in just one of these spaces? Then, for a rest-to-rest move along that line, contrast a trapezoidal velocity profile with a min-jerk profile: sketch both velocity shapes, say what each demands of acceleration at the phase switches, and qualify what 'infinite jerk' means for the ideal model versus real hardware.
rubric: specifies the waypoints in task space but computes the commands via IK along the path and closes the servo loop in joint space on angle error
justifies the split: straight lines are simple in task space but curved in joint space, while the motors and sensors live in joint space, so neither space alone suffices

contrasts the profiles: the ideal trapezoid switches acceleration stepwise, giving unbounded jerk spikes in the ideal model (large but finite spikes on smoothed real hardware), while min-jerk ramps acceleration continuously with bounded jerk
motion-ik-taskspace.transfer_probe: A passenger elevator must run a timed floor-to-floor trip with a comfortable ride. Where is the ride specified (floor heights versus motor shaft turns), where is the motor actually servoed, and why the split — and why does an S-curve (min-jerk-like) profile beat an ideal trapezoid for comfort, including what 'infinite jerk' means for the ideal model versus the real drive?

pendulum-cart-instability.claim: The inverted pendulum is unstable because a small tilt produces a gravity torque that enlarges the tilt with no restoring force, so it falls on a timescale of order sqrt(L/g) and any balancing controller must sense and push back well within that time.
pendulum-cart-instability.probe: A 0.5-m stick balances upright on your palm (use g = 9.81 m/s²). Explain why the upright position is unstable rather than stable, compute the approximate fall timescale sqrt(L/g) for this stick, and state the quantitative timing requirement this imposes on any controller (or your hand) trying to keep it up.
rubric: explains instability: a tilt creates a gravity torque that grows the tilt further, with no restoring force (unlike the hanging pendulum)
computes the fall timescale sqrt(0.5/9.81) ≈ 0.22–0.23 s
states the timing requirement: the controller must sense and push back well within ~0.2 s (control loop much faster, tens of ms — not slower than the fall)
pendulum-cart-instability.transfer_probe: A Segway carrying a tall heavy rider tips a few degrees from vertical, and later the same Segway carrying a short light load tips by the same few degrees. Which one falls faster from that tilt, why, and what does the difference demand of the controller's reaction speed in each case?

pendulum-cart-lqr.claim: Cart-pole LQR feeds back the full state (cart position, cart velocity, pole angle, pole angular rate) — the rate terms let it anticipate motion — and its Q and R weights select a point on the pole-angle precision versus cart-travel and control-effort tradeoff.
pendulum-cart-lqr.probe: For a cart-pole driven by LQR: list the four entries of the state vector, explain why the two rate entries are needed rather than positions alone, and state the named tradeoff the Q and R weights choose — then say which way you turn the weights to hold the pole tighter and what you pay for it.
rubric: names the full state vector: cart position x, cart velocity v, pole angle θ, pole angular rate θ̇
explains the rate terms: they let the controller anticipate/predict motion direction and damp it, rather than reacting only to static position error

states the tradeoff as pole-angle precision versus cart-travel/control effort: Q penalizes state error, R penalizes effort, so raising Q relative to R holds the pole tighter at the cost of larger, more aggressive cart excursions and effort
pendulum-cart-lqr.transfer_probe: You balance a broom on your palm and choose between keeping the broom almost perfectly vertical with big fast hand sprints versus letting it lean and wobble more while your hand barely moves. Name the tradeoff you are choosing, say which position and rate readings your eyes and hand must track to do either, and which strategy matches turning Q up relative to R.

capstone.claim: You can USE Mechatronics Spine — frames, kinematics, dynamics & integration in your own work, not just explain it.
capstone.probe: Build the thing. In your real repo, your real notes, your real argument — produce something that only works if you actually understand Mechatronics Spine — frames, kinematics, dynamics & integration. Your stated goal: The integration backbone of the vault's Mechatronics roadmap (Mechatronics/ROADMAP.md): coordinate frames -> FK -> IK, the calculus/bond-graph modeling language, dynamics (pendulum family), impedance interaction, and Phase-4 integration artifacts (harness/workcell, gripper/tool-changer). Discipline detail lives in sibling trees: mech-software, mech-electronics, mech-mechanical, mech-project-safety. Cross-tree prerequisites are named inside node claims (engram edges are intra-graph only); the milestone/tag system remains the operating manual.. Ship it, then explain which concept made which decision.
rubric: the artifact exists and works (or the argument stands on its own)
names at least two concepts from this topic that DECIDED something in it
identifies where the model broke down or needed more than the topic gave
